Result Cache — stores query results for 24 hours; exact same SQL against unchanged data reuses the result for free. 3. Local Disk Cache (per warehouse) — caches raw column data read from storage; shared across queries on the same warehouse.

cards.q: What is a micro-partition in Snowflake?
cards.a: The fundamental storage unit. Data is automatically divided into immutable, compressed, columnar files of 50–500 MB (uncompressed). Each micro-partition stores min/max statistics per column, enabling Snowflake to prune (skip) partitions that can't satisfy a query's predicates.

cards.q: What are the four table types in Snowflake?
cards.a: Permanent (default) — full Time Travel + 7-day Fail-Safe. Temporary — session-scoped, auto-dropped; 0 or 1-day Time Travel, no Fail-Safe. Transient — survives sessions but 0-day Fail-Safe; lower storage cost. External — references files in cloud storage; read-only, no Time Travel.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Temporary table?
cards.a: A table that exists only for the current session. It is automatically dropped when the session ends. Temporary tables are invisible to other sessions and have 0 or 1-day Time Travel but no Fail-Safe period.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Transient table and when would you use one?
cards.a: A table with no Fail-Safe (0-day) and 0–1 day Time Travel. Use it for staging or intermediary data that doesn't need long-term protection — it reduces storage costs compared with permanent tables.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake External Table?
cards.a: A read-only table that queries files stored in an external stage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) without ingesting the data into Snowflake. Useful for querying data-lake files in-place. No Time Travel or Fail-Safe.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Materialized View?
cards.a: A pre-computed view whose results are stored physically and refreshed automatically by Snowflake when the underlying base table changes. Faster to query than a standard view because data is pre-aggregated, but incurs storage and maintenance compute cost.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Sequence?
cards.a: An object that generates unique, monotonically increasing integer values. Used to create surrogate keys: NEXTVAL for the sequence is called in INSERT statements. Note: values are guaranteed unique but NOT guaranteed to be gap-free.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Stage?
cards.a: A named location that holds data files before loading (or after unloading). Internal stages are managed by Snowflake (user stage @~, table stage @%table, named stage). External stages point to cloud object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob).

cards.q: What is Snowflake Time Travel?
cards.a: A feature that lets you query, clone, or restore data from a past point in time — using AT(TIMESTAMP), AT(OFFSET), or AT(STATEMENT). Retention is 0–1 day for Standard edition and 0–90 days for Enterprise edition.

cards.q: What is Snowflake Fail-Safe?
cards.a: A 7-day non-configurable recovery window that begins after the Time Travel retention period expires. It is a Snowflake-managed disaster recovery mechanism — users cannot query or restore data themselves; only Snowflake support can recover it.

cards.q: What is Zero-Copy Cloning?
cards.a: Instantly creates a copy of a table, schema, or database by pointing to the same underlying micro-partitions — no data is physically duplicated at clone time. The clone and original diverge as changes are made, sharing only unchanged micro-partitions.

cards.q: Can you clone a table at a historical point in time?
cards.a: Yes. CREATE TABLE my_clone CLONE my_table AT(TIMESTAMP => '2024-01-01 00:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ); The clone reflects the state of the table at that past moment (within the Time Travel window).

cards.q: What is RBAC in Snowflake?
cards.a: Role-Based Access Control — privileges are granted to roles (not directly to users), and roles are granted to users. A user can hold multiple roles and switches between them. All objects are owned by a role.

cards.q: What are the five built-in Snowflake system roles?
cards.a: ACCOUNTADMIN — top-level, full control. SYSADMIN — creates and manages warehouses/databases/objects. SECURITYADMIN — manages users, roles, and grants. USERADMIN — creates and manages users and roles. PUBLIC — automatically granted to every user; minimal privileges.

cards.q: What does the ACCOUNTADMIN role do?
cards.a: The most powerful role. It can manage all account-level settings, billing, resource monitors, and can GRANT any privilege. Should be granted to as few users as possible. Snowflake best practice: never use it for day-to-day work.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Resource Monitor?
cards.a: An object that tracks credit consumption by virtual warehouses. You set thresholds (e.g., 80%, 100%) and choose actions: notify, notify and suspend, or notify and suspend immediately. Prevents runaway warehouse spend.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Network Policy?
cards.a: A policy that restricts Snowflake account or user access based on IP address. You define an ALLOWED_IP_LIST (and optionally BLOCKED_IP_LIST). Can be applied at account or user level.

cards.q: What is the COPY INTO <table> command?
cards.a: The primary bulk-loading command. It copies data from a stage into a Snowflake table. Supports CSV, JSON, Avro, ORC, Parquet, and XML. Options include ON_ERROR (continue/skip_file/abort_statement), PURGE, and VALIDATION_MODE.

cards.q: What is Snowpipe?
cards.a: Snowflake's continuous, serverless data ingestion service. When new files land in a cloud storage location (triggered via SQS/event notification or a REST API call), Snowpipe automatically loads them into the target table — typically within minutes.

cards.q: What is the difference between bulk loading (COPY INTO) and Snowpipe?
cards.a: Bulk loading uses a customer-managed virtual warehouse and is best for large, scheduled batch loads. Snowpipe is serverless (Snowflake-managed compute) and triggers on file arrival — best for continuous, low-latency micro-batch ingestion.

cards.q: What is the PUT command in Snowflake?
cards.a: Uploads files from a local file system to a Snowflake internal stage. Only available via the SnowSQL CLI or drivers — not in the Snowsight web UI. Usage: PUT file:///path/to/file @my_stage;

cards.q: What is the GET command in Snowflake?
cards.a: Downloads files from a Snowflake internal stage to a local file system. Like PUT, only available via SnowSQL or drivers. Usage: GET @my_stage/file.csv file:///local/path/;

cards.q: What data type does Snowflake use to store semi-structured data?
cards.a: VARIANT — a flexible, self-describing column that can hold any JSON, XML, Avro, ORC, or Parquet value up to 16 MB. Snowflake automatically extracts and stores typed columns internally for efficient querying.

cards.q: How do you access a nested JSON key in a Snowflake VARIANT column?
cards.a: Using colon notation: column:key or column:key:nested_key. For example: SELECT src:address:city FROM my_table; Arrays use bracket notation: src:items[0]:price. Column names in the path are case-sensitive.

cards.q: What does PARSE_JSON() do in Snowflake?
cards.a: Converts a VARCHAR string containing a JSON document into a VARIANT value so you can traverse it with colon notation. Example: SELECT PARSE_JSON('{"id": 1}'):id::INT;

cards.q: What is FLATTEN in Snowflake?
cards.a: A table function that explodes arrays or objects in a VARIANT column into one row per element. Use it with LATERAL to join the expanded rows back to the outer query. Commonly used for processing JSON arrays.

cards.q: What is Snowflake Secure Data Sharing?
cards.a: Lets you share live, read-only access to Snowflake objects (tables, views, UDFs) with other Snowflake accounts without copying or moving data. Sharing works at the micro-partition level — consumers always see up-to-date data.

cards.q: What is the Snowflake Marketplace?
cards.a: A platform built on Secure Data Sharing where data providers publish live datasets and consumers discover and access them — free or paid. Consumers access data directly in their own Snowflake account with no ETL.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Reader Account?
cards.a: A Snowflake-managed account created by a data provider for a consumer who doesn't have their own Snowflake account. The provider pays for the Reader Account's compute. The consumer can only access data shared by that provider.

cards.q: What is query pruning in Snowflake?
cards.a: Before scanning data, Snowflake uses the min/max column statistics stored per micro-partition to skip partitions that cannot satisfy the query's WHERE predicates. The fewer micro-partitions scanned, the faster and cheaper the query.

cards.q: What is spilling to disk and why is it a performance problem?
cards.a: When an operation (sort, join, aggregation) requires more memory than the warehouse has available, Snowflake spills intermediate results to local SSD, then to remote cloud storage if SSD is also exhausted. Remote spill is very slow — it indicates the warehouse needs to be sized up.

cards.q: What is the result cache and when does it NOT apply?
cards.a: The result cache stores query results for 24 hours in the Cloud Services Layer. It does NOT apply when: the underlying table data has changed, the query uses non-deterministic functions (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, RANDOM, SEQ), or the query uses columns with row access policies.

cards.q: What is the local disk cache (data cache) in Snowflake?
cards.a: Each virtual warehouse maintains an SSD cache of column data it has read from cloud storage during the current session. Subsequent queries on the same warehouse that access the same data can read from this cache instead of cloud storage — much faster. Cleared when the warehouse suspends.

cards.q: What is the Snowflake Cloud Services Layer responsible for?
cards.a: Authentication and authorisation, metadata management (table definitions, statistics, micro-partition maps), query parsing and optimisation (producing the query plan), and transaction management (ACID guarantees). It runs continuously — no warehouse is needed for its operations.

cards.q: How does Snowflake achieve ACID transactions?
cards.a: Through the Cloud Services Layer, which manages multi-version concurrency control (MVCC). Writers create new micro-partitions (old ones are immutable); readers see a consistent snapshot. This allows concurrent reads and writes without blocking.

cards.q: What is a Clustering Key in Snowflake?
cards.a: One or more columns (or expressions) declared on a table that Snowflake uses to co-locate related data in the same micro-partitions. Well-chosen clustering keys improve pruning for queries that filter on those columns, reducing scan size and cost.

cards.q: What is Automatic Clustering in Snowflake?
cards.a: A Snowflake-managed background service that continuously reorganises the data in a clustered table so it remains well-clustered over time — especially after heavy DML. It consumes compute credits and is billed separately from virtual warehouses.

cards.q: How do you choose a good clustering key?
cards.a: Choose columns that are: (1) frequently used in WHERE / JOIN predicates, (2) high-cardinality but with locality (dates, region codes), (3) not too many — 1-3 columns is typical. Avoid high-cardinality columns like UUIDs or columns never filtered on.

cards.q: What are SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION() and SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_DEPTH()?
cards.a: System functions that report clustering quality. CLUSTERING_DEPTH returns the average depth of overlapping micro-partitions on a key — lower is better (1.0 = perfectly clustered). CLUSTERING_INFORMATION gives a JSON breakdown of the distribution.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Stream?
cards.a: A Change Data Capture (CDC) object that records INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations made to a source table since the last time the stream was consumed. Reading the stream (via DML) advances its offset.

cards.q: What columns does a Snowflake Stream add to each row?
cards.a: METADATA$ACTION — INSERT or DELETE. METADATA$ISUPDATE — TRUE if the row is part of an UPDATE (updates appear as a DELETE + INSERT pair). METADATA$ROW_ID — a unique row identifier for the source row.

cards.q: What are the three types of Snowflake Streams?
cards.a: Standard — captures all DML (insert/update/delete) on a table. Append-only — captures only INSERTs; more efficient for insert-only sources (e.g., event logs). Insert-only (on external tables) — tracks new files added to an external stage.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Task?
cards.a: A scheduled object that executes a single SQL statement or a call to a stored procedure. Tasks can be chained into DAGs using the AFTER clause. A root task has a CRON schedule; child tasks trigger when their parent succeeds.

cards.q: What is the relationship between Streams and Tasks in Snowflake?
cards.a: A common pattern: a Task checks SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('my_stream') and runs a MERGE or INSERT from the stream into a target table. The Task consumes the stream, advancing its offset. This creates a lightweight incremental pipeline without external orchestration.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Dynamic Table?
cards.a: A table whose contents are automatically refreshed by Snowflake based on a declarative query (like a materialised view). Unlike tasks+streams, you write the transformation logic once; Snowflake determines what changed and refreshes incrementally. Introduced as a simpler alternative to task DAGs.

cards.q: What is LATERAL FLATTEN and how is it different from plain FLATTEN?
cards.a: LATERAL FLATTEN joins the output of the FLATTEN table function back to each outer row. Without LATERAL, you'd write: FROM my_table, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => my_table.data:items). With LATERAL it's implicit: SELECT f.value FROM my_table, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => data:items) f. The LATERAL keyword is often optional in Snowflake syntax.

cards.q: What is OBJECT_CONSTRUCT() in Snowflake?
cards.a: Builds a VARIANT object from key-value pairs at query time: OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('id', 1, 'name', 'Alice'). Useful for assembling JSON output in SELECT statements or for feeding downstream VARIANT columns.

cards.q: What is ARRAY_AGG() in Snowflake?
cards.a: An aggregate function that collects column values into a VARIANT ARRAY. Often combined with OBJECT_CONSTRUCT to produce nested JSON output: SELECT ARRAY_AGG(OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('id', id, 'name', name)) FROM my_table;

cards.q: What does the :: operator do in Snowflake?
cards.a: Casts a VARIANT value to a SQL type: src:price::FLOAT, src:created_at::TIMESTAMP_NTZ. Without casting, Snowflake keeps the value as VARIANT, which may cause unexpected comparison behaviour.

cards.q: What file formats can Snowflake ingest natively into VARIANT columns?
cards.a: JSON, XML, Avro, ORC, and Parquet. COPY INTO automatically stores each top-level record as one VARIANT row when the file format is set to JSON/Avro/etc. CSV is not semi-structured and loads into individual typed columns.

cards.q: What is Dynamic Data Masking in Snowflake?
cards.a: A column-level security feature that applies a masking policy to a column. Users with privileged roles see real data; others see masked data (e.g., NULL, a fixed string, or a partially masked value). The masking is applied at query time — data on disk is unchanged.

cards.q: What is a Row Access Policy in Snowflake?
cards.a: Attaches a policy function to a table or view that filters rows returned to a user based on their role or session context. The filter is transparent — users with restricted access see fewer rows but aren't aware of the filtering.

cards.q: What is Snowflake's approach to encryption?
cards.a: All data at rest is encrypted with AES-256. All data in transit uses TLS. Snowflake manages encryption keys automatically (Snowflake-managed keys). Business Critical and VPS editions support customer-managed keys via Tri-Secret Secure (a key held jointly by Snowflake and the customer).

cards.q: What is Tri-Secret Secure in Snowflake?
cards.a: A Business Critical/VPS feature that combines a Snowflake-managed key with a customer-managed key (held in AWS KMS/Azure Key Vault/GCP KMS). Both keys are required to decrypt data — Snowflake alone cannot access it without the customer's key.

cards.q: What is column-level security in Snowflake?
cards.a: The ability to restrict access to specific columns using Dynamic Data Masking policies or by granting SELECT on individual columns (not the whole table). Privilege: GRANT SELECT (col1, col2) ON TABLE my_table TO ROLE analyst;

cards.q: What is the Search Optimization Service in Snowflake?
cards.a: An optional, paid table-level service that builds a search access path for selective equality and range queries on high-cardinality columns. Particularly useful for queries like WHERE id = 'some-uuid' that would otherwise scan many micro-partitions.

cards.q: What is a Query Profile in Snowflake?
cards.a: A graphical execution plan available in Snowsight showing each operator in the query, how long it took, rows processed, and bytes scanned. Key things to look for: spill to disk, large CartesianJoin, exploding joins, and which step is the bottleneck.

cards.q: When should you increase Virtual Warehouse size vs. add more clusters?
cards.a: Increase size (scale up) when individual queries are slow — they need more CPU/memory per query. Add clusters (scale out) when many users are queued and individual query speed is fine — they need more concurrent capacity.

cards.q: What is warehouse query queuing in Snowflake?
cards.a: When a single-cluster warehouse is at full concurrency, incoming queries queue. In Snowsight you can see queue time in the query history. Solutions: scale up the warehouse, enable multi-cluster, or route query types to separate warehouses.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Resource Monitor and how does it help cost control?
cards.a: A Resource Monitor tracks credit usage by one or more virtual warehouses against a quota. When the quota reaches a threshold (e.g., 90%), it can notify, suspend, or immediately suspend the warehouse. Prevents unexpected runaway costs.

cards.q: What is database replication in Snowflake?
cards.a: A feature that replicates a database (or account objects) from a primary account to one or more secondary accounts in different regions or cloud providers. Used for read-scale, disaster recovery, and cross-region data sharing.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Failover Group?
cards.a: A group of account objects (databases, integrations, warehouses) that can be failed over together from a primary to a secondary account. On failover, the secondary becomes the new primary and handles reads and writes.

cards.q: Write a COPY INTO statement that loads all CSV files from the named internal stage @my_stage into the table 'raw_events'. Use the file format 'my_csv_format' and skip the first header row.
cards.a:
```sql
COPY INTO raw_events
FROM @my_stage
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'my_csv_format')
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';
```
cards.explanation: This COPY INTO statement loads data from a Snowflake internal stage into a table by specifying the target table `raw_events` and the source location `@my_stage`, which references the named internal stage. The `FILE_FORMAT` clause points to a pre-defined format object `my_csv_format` that already contains the CSV parsing rules, including the header row skip setting—this is why the SKIP_HEADER parameter isn't explicitly repeated here, as it's configured within the format definition itself. The `ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'` directive tells Snowflake to proceed loading remaining files even if some files encounter errors, preventing the entire operation from failing on a single bad file. This approach is efficient because named file formats are reusable across multiple COPY operations and centralize format configuration, reducing redundancy and ensuring consistency.

cards.q: Create a named internal stage called 'events_stage' with a CSV file format that uses comma delimiter, double-quote string delimiter, and skips one header line.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE STAGE events_stage
  FILE_FORMAT = (
    TYPE = 'CSV'
    FIELD_DELIMITER = ','
    FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
    SKIP_HEADER = 1
  );
```
cards.explanation: This code creates an internal stage in Snowflake—a named location for storing files—with a specific CSV parsing configuration. The `CREATE STAGE events_stage` command establishes the stage itself without specifying an external location, making it internal by default. The `FILE_FORMAT` clause embeds format specifications directly, defining how Snowflake should parse files uploaded to this stage. `TYPE = 'CSV'` sets the expected file format, while `FIELD_DELIMITER = ','` tells Snowflake that commas separate columns in the data. `FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'` means fields can be wrapped in double quotes, which is important for handling values that contain commas or special characters without breaking the parsing logic. Finally, `SKIP_HEADER = 1` instructs Snowflake to ignore the first line of each file, which typically contains column names. By defining these format rules at stage creation, any COPY command referencing this stage will automatically apply these settings, eliminating the need to repeat them for every data load.

cards.q: Create an external stage called 's3_stage' pointing to an S3 bucket, using a storage integration called 'my_s3_integration'.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE STAGE s3_stage
  URL = 's3://my-bucket/data/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = my_s3_integration
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'JSON');
```
cards.explanation: This SQL statement creates a named stage object in Snowflake that acts as a reference point for loading or unloading data from S3. The `URL` parameter specifies the exact S3 bucket path where files are stored, and `STORAGE_INTEGRATION = my_s3_integration` delegates authentication to a previously configured storage integration rather than embedding credentials directly in the stage definition—this is a security best practice because it centralizes credential management. The `FILE_FORMAT` clause pre-defines how Snowflake should interpret files loaded through this stage, so you don't need to specify the format every time you reference the stage in a COPY or SELECT statement. Once created, you can reference this stage by name (e.g., `@s3_stage`) in data movement operations, making your code cleaner and more maintainable.

cards.q: Write a query that reads the 'user_id' (integer) and 'event_name' (string) fields from a VARIANT column called 'raw' in the table 'events'.
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT
    raw:user_id::INT        AS user_id,
    raw:event_name::VARCHAR AS event_name
FROM events;
```
cards.explanation: This query extracts nested fields from a VARIANT column using Snowflake's dot notation syntax. The `raw:user_id` and `raw:event_name` expressions access the `user_id` and `event_name` keys within the JSON-like VARIANT object. The `::INT` and `::VARCHAR` cast operators then convert those semi-structured values into their proper SQL types—integers and strings respectively—so they can be reliably used in downstream queries and aggregations. The `AS` aliases rename the extracted columns to their final names in the result set, making the output clean and explicit.

cards.q: Use LATERAL FLATTEN to explode a JSON array at src:items into one row per item, selecting item:product_id and item:quantity from the 'orders' table.
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    f.value:product_id::INT      AS product_id,
    f.value:quantity::INT        AS quantity
FROM orders o,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => o.src:items) f;
```
cards.explanation: This query uses Snowflake's `LATERAL FLATTEN` function to decompose a JSON array into individual rows. The `LATERAL` keyword allows the `FLATTEN` function to reference `o.src:items` from the outer `orders` table, essentially performing a join where each array element becomes a separate output row. The `input => o.src:items` parameter specifies which JSON array to expand, and the alias `f` labels the flattened results so you can reference them in the SELECT clause. The `f.value` expression accesses each individual item in the array, and the `::INT` casts convert the JSON values to integer type since Snowflake preserves JSON data types by default. By selecting `o.order_id` alongside the flattened item fields, you maintain the relationship between parent orders and their exploded line items.

cards.q: Write a Time Travel query that shows what the 'customers' table looked like 2 hours ago.
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers
AT (OFFSET => -60 * 60 * 2);
```
cards.explanation: This Snowflake Time Travel query retrieves a historical snapshot of the `customers` table from two hours in the past. The `AT` clause with the `OFFSET` parameter specifies a point in time relative to the current moment, measured in seconds. The calculation `-60 * 60 * 2` converts two hours into negative seconds (negative because you're going backward in time): 60 seconds per minute × 60 minutes per hour × 2 hours = 7,200 seconds ago. Snowflake's Time Travel feature keeps versions of tables available for a default retention period (typically 24 hours for standard edition), allowing you to query historical data without needing separate audit tables or change data capture logic.

cards.q: Write a Time Travel query that restores the 'orders' table to its state before a specific statement ran (using the query ID).
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE orders
  CLONE orders
  BEFORE (STATEMENT => '01ab2cd3-0004-5678-0000-000000000000');
```
cards.explanation: This query uses Snowflake's Time Travel feature with the CLONE command to restore a table to a point in time before a specific statement executed. The `BEFORE (STATEMENT => '...')` clause tells Snowflake to look up the exact timestamp when that query ID ran, then clone the table as it existed just before that statement modified it. By using `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE orders CLONE orders`, you're replacing the current (potentially corrupted or incorrectly modified) orders table with a clean copy from the past. The statement ID acts as a precise anchor point—more specific than using a timestamp directly—because it automatically resolves to the exact moment before that DML operation took effect. This is particularly useful when you know exactly which query caused the problem but need to recover data without manually calculating timestamps.

cards.q: Create a zero-copy clone of the 'production' database named 'dev'.
cards.explanation: This statement creates a new database called `dev` that is an instant, zero-copy clone of the `production` database. The `CLONE` keyword (supported in Snowflake) creates a copy of all schemas, tables, and other objects without duplicating the underlying data—instead, the clone shares the same micro-partitions as the source through copy-on-write semantics. This approach is extremely efficient because it requires minimal storage overhead and completes nearly instantaneously, regardless of the source database size. When you modify data in either the original or cloned database, Snowflake creates new micro-partitions only for the changed data, keeping the clone and source completely independent while conserving space.

cards.q: Create a stream called 'orders_stream' on the 'orders' table that captures all changes (standard stream).
cards.explanation: This statement creates a standard stream object named `orders_stream` that tracks all data changes (inserts, updates, and deletes) on the `orders` table. The `ON TABLE` clause specifies which table the stream monitors—in this case, `orders`. When you query this stream, Snowflake returns only the rows that changed since the last time the stream was consumed, along with metadata columns (`METADATA$ACTION` and `METADATA$ISUPDATE`) that indicate what type of change occurred. Standard streams capture all DML operations by default, making them useful for ETL pipelines that need to process incremental changes without rescanning the entire table. Since no stream type is explicitly specified, Snowflake creates a standard stream rather than an append-only or insert-only variant.

cards.q: Write a MERGE statement that reads from 'orders_stream' and upserts into 'orders_target': insert new rows (METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT') and delete removed rows.
cards.a:
```sql
MERGE INTO orders_target t
USING (
    SELECT * FROM orders_stream
    WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' OR METADATA$ISUPDATE
) s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = s.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, status) VALUES (s.order_id, s.status);
```
cards.explanation: The MERGE statement begins by targeting the `orders_target` table and aliasing it as `t`, while the USING clause filters the `orders_stream` to capture only relevant changes—either new inserts (`METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'`) or updates (`METADATA$ISUPDATE`). The ON clause establishes the join condition using `order_id` to determine which rows in the target already exist. When a match is found (WHEN MATCHED), the UPDATE clause modifies the `status` column in the target table to reflect the stream's current value, effectively handling updates to existing orders. When no match is found (WHEN NOT MATCHED), the INSERT clause adds the new order as a complete row into the target table, growing the dataset with incoming data. This two-pronged approach ensures the target table stays synchronized with the stream by both refreshing changed records and absorbing new ones in a single atomic operation.

cards.q: Create a Task that runs every hour, checks if orders_stream has data, and calls a stored procedure to process it.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE TASK process_orders
  WAREHOUSE = my_wh
  SCHEDULE = 'USING CRON 0 * * * * UTC'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('orders_stream')
AS
  CALL process_new_orders();

ALTER TASK process_orders RESUME;
```
cards.explanation: This code creates a Snowflake Task that automates order processing on an hourly cadence. The `SCHEDULE` clause with CRON syntax `0 * * * * UTC` triggers the task at the start of every hour in UTC timezone. The `WHEN` clause contains a crucial conditional check using `SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA()` — this function evaluates to true only if the specified stream has captured changes, preventing unnecessary executions when there's no new data to process. The task executes a stored procedure `process_new_orders()` that handles the actual data transformation, and the `WAREHOUSE` parameter specifies which compute resources to use. Finally, `ALTER TASK process_orders RESUME` activates the task since newly created tasks are suspended by default — without this statement, the task would never run despite being properly configured.

cards.q: Write a query using the QUALIFY clause to return only the most recent order per customer (using ROW_NUMBER).
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    order_id,
    order_date
FROM orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1;
```
cards.explanation: The QUALIFY clause filters rows based on window function results, acting as a WHERE clause for window functions. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) assigns a sequential number to each order within each customer's group, ordered by date from newest to oldest, so the most recent order gets rank 1. The QUALIFY condition = 1 keeps only those rows with rank 1, effectively returning a single row per customer—the one with the most recent order_date. This approach is cleaner than wrapping the query in a CTE or subquery because QUALIFY eliminates the need for an outer SELECT, making the intent immediately clear.

cards.q: Write a query using SAMPLE to return approximately 10% of rows from 'events' (Bernoulli sampling).
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM events
SAMPLE BERNOULLI (10);
```
cards.explanation: The `SAMPLE BERNOULLI (10)` clause uses Bernoulli sampling to randomly select rows from the `events` table with approximately a 10% probability. Bernoulli sampling evaluates each row independently and includes it in the result set based on the specified percentage, making it ideal when you want a truly random subset rather than systematic sampling. The percentage argument (10) represents the probability that any given row will be included, so higher values return more rows. This method is efficient for large tables because it doesn't require sorting or scanning the entire dataset before filtering—each row's inclusion is determined on the fly during table scan.

cards.q: Create a simple JavaScript UDF called 'add_tax' that takes a price FLOAT and returns price * 1.2.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION add_tax(price FLOAT)
RETURNS FLOAT
LANGUAGE JAVASCRIPT
AS $$
  return PRICE * 1.2;
$$;
```
cards.explanation: This creates a reusable JavaScript User-Defined Function in Snowflake that multiplies an input price by 1.2 to calculate a price-inclusive tax amount. The `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` statement defines the function name and its parameter (`price` as FLOAT), while `RETURNS FLOAT` specifies the output type. The `LANGUAGE JAVASCRIPT` clause tells Snowflake to execute the code block as JavaScript rather than SQL, and the dollar-sign delimiters `$$` mark the boundaries of the JavaScript code body. Inside the function, `PRICE` (uppercase) refers to the parameter value—Snowflake converts parameter names to uppercase by default—and the `return` statement passes the calculated result back to the caller. Once created, you can call this function in any SQL query like `SELECT add_tax(100)` to get 120.

cards.q: Create a masking policy called 'mask_email' that shows the real email to users with the ANALYST role, and returns '***' to everyone else. Then apply it to the 'email' column on 'customers'.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE MASKING POLICY mask_email AS (val STRING)
RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE
    WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'ANALYST' THEN val
    ELSE '***'
  END;

ALTER TABLE customers
  MODIFY COLUMN email SET MASKING POLICY mask_email;
```
cards.explanation: The first statement creates a masking policy by defining a function-like structure that evaluates access at query time. The `AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING ->` syntax establishes that the policy receives a string value and returns a string, with the arrow indicating the conditional logic that follows. The `CASE` statement checks `CURRENT_ROLE()`, a Snowflake function that returns the role of the user executing the query, and returns the unmasked original value `val` only when the role matches 'ANALYST', otherwise returning the literal string '***' for all other roles. The second statement applies this policy to the `email` column on the `customers` table using `ALTER TABLE` with the `MODIFY COLUMN` clause, which tells Snowflake to enforce the masking policy on that specific column whenever it's queried. This approach ensures dynamic masking—the same query returns different data based on who runs it—without requiring separate tables or views for different user groups.

cards.q: Create a Resource Monitor called 'monthly_cap' with a 1000-credit monthly quota that suspends all warehouses at 100% and sends a notification at 80%.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR monthly_cap
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 1000
       FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
       START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS
    ON 80  PERCENT DO NOTIFY
    ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
```
cards.explanation: This SQL statement creates a Snowflake Resource Monitor that enforces credit consumption limits and automated responses. The `WITH` clause establishes the foundational parameters: `CREDIT_QUOTA = 1000` sets the monthly spending limit to 1000 credits, `FREQUENCY = MONTHLY` resets the quota every calendar month, and `START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY` activates the monitor right away without waiting for a scheduled time. The `TRIGGERS` section defines two escalating actions: the first trigger fires at 80 percent consumption and executes `NOTIFY`, which sends an alert to account administrators as an early warning before the limit is reached, while the second trigger activates at 100 percent and executes `SUSPEND`, which immediately halts all warehouses to prevent further credit overage. This two-tier approach balances operational awareness with cost control by giving teams visibility of approaching limits while ultimately preventing uncontrolled spending.

cards.q: Write a Snowpipe definition (CREATE PIPE) that auto-ingest files from an S3 stage into the 'events' table.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE PIPE events_pipe
  AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
AS
  COPY INTO events
  FROM @s3_stage
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'JSON');
```
cards.explanation: This Snowpipe definition automatically ingests JSON files from an S3 stage into the events table. The `AUTO_INGEST = TRUE` parameter enables the pipe to listen for S3 notifications and trigger ingestion whenever new files arrive, eliminating the need for manual refresh commands. The `COPY INTO events FROM @s3_stage` statement specifies the target table and source stage, while `FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'JSON')` tells Snowpipe how to parse the incoming data. By naming the pipe `events_pipe`, you create a referenceable object that Snowflake uses internally to track ingestion history and manage the auto-loading process.

cards.q: Write a PIVOT query that turns status values ('placed','shipped','returned') into columns, counting orders per customer.
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, status FROM orders
)
PIVOT (COUNT(*) FOR status IN ('placed', 'shipped', 'returned'))
  AS p (customer_id, placed, shipped, returned);
```
cards.explanation: The PIVOT clause reorganizes rows into columns by aggregating data based on specified values. The subquery first selects the two columns needed—customer_id and status—then PIVOT counts how many times each status appears for each customer. The FOR status IN (...) clause tells the database which column to pivot on (status) and which distinct values ('placed', 'shipped', 'returned') should become new column names. The AS p (...) clause aliases the pivoted result and explicitly names the output columns: customer_id remains as-is, while the three status values each become their own column containing the COUNT(*) aggregate. Finally, SELECT * retrieves all columns from the pivoted result, giving you one row per customer with order counts spread across the status columns.

cards.q: Use OBJECT_CONSTRUCT and ARRAY_AGG to build a JSON array of {order_id, amount} objects grouped by customer_id.
cards.a:
```sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    ARRAY_AGG(
        OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('order_id', order_id, 'amount', amount)
    ) AS orders_json
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```
cards.explanation: This query groups orders by customer and creates a JSON representation of each customer's order history. `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` builds individual JSON objects for each row by pairing the keys `'order_id'` and `'amount'` with their corresponding column values, creating objects like `{"order_id": 123, "amount": 45.99}`. `ARRAY_AGG` then aggregates all these individual objects into a single JSON array per customer, so each row in the result contains one customer_id paired with a complete array of their orders. The `GROUP BY customer_id` clause ensures that orders are properly partitioned by customer before aggregation occurs, preventing data from different customers from being mixed together in a single array.

cards.q: Write a Dynamic Table definition that materialises a daily summary of revenue by product, refreshing when data is at most 1 hour stale.
cards.a:
```sql
CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE product_revenue_daily
  TARGET_LAG = '1 hour'
  WAREHOUSE = my_wh
AS
  SELECT
      product_id,
      DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date) AS order_day,
      SUM(amount)                  AS daily_revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1, 2;
```
cards.explanation: A Dynamic Table automatically maintains materialized results and refreshes based on staleness thresholds rather than fixed schedules. The `TARGET_LAG = '1 hour'` clause specifies that Snowflake should refresh this table whenever the underlying data becomes more than 1 hour out of sync, ensuring near-real-time aggregations without manual refresh triggers. The `WAREHOUSE = my_wh` parameter designates which compute cluster handles these incremental refreshes efficiently. The query itself groups orders by product and day, using `DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date)` to normalize timestamps to daily boundaries so that multiple orders within the same day aggregate into a single row per product. `SUM(amount)` calculates total revenue for each product-day combination, and the `GROUP BY 1, 2` refers to the first two selected columns, making the query more maintainable. This approach eliminates the need for scheduled tasks or manual updates — Snowflake tracks source table changes and refreshes intelligently based on your staleness tolerance.

cards.q: What separates Snowflake's architecture from shared-disk and shared-nothing architectures?
cards.a: Snowflake uses a hybrid: storage is shared (centralised cloud object storage accessed by all compute) like shared-disk, but compute nodes (virtual warehouses) are independent MPP clusters that don't share memory or CPU, like shared-nothing. This gives both storage elasticity and compute isolation.

cards.q: Can multiple virtual warehouses access the same data simultaneously in Snowflake?
cards.a: Yes. Because storage and compute are decoupled, any number of virtual warehouses can read from the same tables concurrently without contention. Each warehouse has its own local disk cache, but underlying storage is shared.

cards.q: What happens to the local disk (data) cache when a virtual warehouse is suspended?
cards.a: It is lost. The cache is stored on the warehouse's local SSDs; suspension deallocates those resources. When the warehouse resumes, the cache starts empty and is rebuilt as queries are executed.

cards.q: What is the maximum Time Travel retention for Enterprise edition?
cards.a: 90 days for permanent tables. Standard edition is limited to 1 day. Temporary and transient tables are limited to 0 or 1 day regardless of edition.

cards.q: What is the Fail-Safe period and who can access data during it?
cards.a: 7 days, non-configurable, beginning after the Time Travel window closes. Only Snowflake Support can recover data during Fail-Safe — it is not user-accessible. It exists as an emergency recovery measure, not a routine tool.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the 60-second minimum warehouse billing?
cards.a: Warehouses are billed for at least 60 seconds each time they start (resume or initial start). After the first 60 seconds, billing is per-second. This means very short queries benefit from keeping warehouses running (or using Snowpark-optimised warehouses with different billing).

cards.q: What are the scaling modes for a multi-cluster warehouse?
cards.a: Auto-scale mode — clusters spin up when queries queue and shut down when load drops (recommended for variable concurrency). Maximised mode — all clusters run at all times (for consistently high concurrency). You set min and max cluster counts.

cards.q: Which Snowflake edition supports multi-cluster virtual warehouses?
cards.a: Enterprise edition and above (Enterprise, Business Critical, VPS). Standard edition supports only single-cluster warehouses.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake account and how does it differ from a database?
cards.a: An account is the top-level entity — it represents a Snowflake subscription tied to a cloud provider and region. It contains all databases, warehouses, users, roles, and other objects. A database is an object within an account that organises schemas and their tables.

cards.q: How does Snowflake combine RBAC and DAC?
cards.a: Snowflake uses RBAC as the primary model (privileges granted to roles, roles granted to users). DAC is layered on top: every object has an owner role, and that role can grant privileges on the object to other roles. The combination is called DAC + RBAC.

cards.q: What is the difference between SECURITYADMIN and USERADMIN?
cards.a: USERADMIN creates and manages users and roles only. SECURITYADMIN inherits USERADMIN's privileges AND can GRANT/REVOKE any privilege on any object in the account — making it effectively a security superuser.

cards.q: What is Federated Authentication / SSO in Snowflake?
cards.a: Allows users to log in to Snowflake using an external Identity Provider (e.g., Okta, Azure AD) via SAML 2.0. Snowflake validates the SAML assertion rather than an internal password. MFA can be enforced by the IdP.

cards.q: What is key-pair authentication in Snowflake?
cards.a: An alternative to password-based authentication where the user authenticates with a private RSA key. Used with programmatic clients (Python, JDBC, ODBC). The public key is registered with the user in Snowflake; the private key stays client-side.

cards.q: What encryption does Snowflake apply by default?
cards.a: AES-256 for data at rest, TLS 1.2+ for data in transit. Encryption is automatic and transparent — all data in Snowflake's storage layer is encrypted using a hierarchy of keys managed by Snowflake.

cards.q: What are Object Tags in Snowflake and how do they relate to governance?
cards.a: String key-value pairs that can be attached to Snowflake objects (tables, columns, warehouses). Used for data classification (e.g., sensitivity: 'PII'), cost tracking, and as selectors for masking policies or row access policies.

cards.q: In what order does Snowflake check caches before going to cloud storage?
cards.a: 1. Result cache (Cloud Services Layer) — if the exact same query was run recently and data hasn't changed, return the cached result immediately. 2. Local disk cache (warehouse SSD) — if the required micro-partitions are already in the warehouse's cache. 3. Cloud storage — fetch the micro-partitions from S3/GCS/Azure.

cards.q: What metrics in a Query Profile indicate that a warehouse is undersized?
cards.a: Spill to local storage and spill to remote storage — these appear as distinct operations in the profile. Remote spill is the worst indicator. Also watch for long Sort or Aggregate steps with high bytes spilled.

cards.q: What is the Search Optimization Service and what types of queries benefit most?
cards.a: A paid table service that builds a secondary search access path for point lookups on high-cardinality columns (e.g., WHERE id = 'uuid'). Queries with highly selective equality/range predicates on non-clustered columns benefit most. Analytic queries with range scans on clustered keys generally don't need it.

cards.q: How does warehouse size affect performance for a complex GROUP BY query?
cards.a: A larger warehouse has more CPU cores and more memory per node. For a memory-intensive GROUP BY on a large dataset, a larger size prevents spilling and completes the aggregation faster. However, for small queries the query may already be fast at XS — upgrading doesn't help.

cards.q: What file formats can COPY INTO load natively?
cards.a: CSV, JSON, Avro, ORC, Parquet, and XML. Snowflake also supports gzip, Bzip2, Brotli, Zstandard, Deflate, and Raw Deflate compression on most formats.

cards.q: What does VALIDATION_MODE in COPY INTO do?
cards.a: Validates the files without loading them. RETURN_ERRORS returns all rows that would fail. RETURN_N_ROWS returns the first N rows that would be loaded. Useful for checking file format issues before committing a load.

cards.q: What does ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE' do in COPY INTO?
cards.a: If any row in a file causes an error, the entire file is skipped (not loaded). Other files in the COPY operation continue. Compare with CONTINUE (skip only the bad row) and ABORT_STATEMENT (stop the whole COPY).

cards.q: What is the PURGE option in COPY INTO?
cards.a: When PURGE = TRUE, Snowflake automatically removes the source files from the stage after a successful load. Reduces storage cost and simplifies pipeline cleanup.

cards.q: What is a file format object in Snowflake?
cards.a: A named, reusable object (CREATE FILE FORMAT) that stores file format settings (type, delimiter, null string, skip_header, etc.). Referenced in COPY INTO and stage definitions by name — avoids repeating settings in every COPY statement.

cards.q: What triggers Snowpipe to load a new file?
cards.a: Either: (1) an event notification from cloud storage (SQS for S3, Azure Event Grid, GCS Pub/Sub) configured to fire when a file lands — AUTO_INGEST=TRUE; or (2) a REST API call to Snowpipe's insertFiles endpoint that explicitly notifies Snowpipe of new files.

cards.q: What SQL languages/constructs can Snowflake UDFs be written in?
cards.a: JavaScript, Python, Java, Scala, and SQL. Table UDFs (UDTFs) return a table instead of a scalar. UDFs are called in SQL like built-in functions.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Stored Procedure and how does it differ from a UDF?
cards.a: A stored procedure encapsulates procedural logic (loops, conditionals, DDL, DML). Unlike UDFs, stored procedures are called with CALL (not in SELECT), can return a single value or nothing, and can run DDL statements. Written in JavaScript, Python, Java, Scala, or Snowflake Scripting (SQL).

cards.q: What does the QUALIFY clause do in Snowflake SQL?
cards.a: Filters rows after window functions are evaluated — analogous to HAVING for aggregates. Eliminates the need for a wrapping subquery: SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM t QUALIFY rn = 1;

cards.q: How do you query a specific index in a JSON array stored in a VARIANT column?
cards.a: Use bracket notation: column:array[0] for the first element, column:array[1] for the second, etc. You can chain: src:items[0]:product_id::INT to get the product_id of the first item and cast it to INT.

cards.q: What objects can be included in a Snowflake Share?
cards.a: Tables, external tables, secure views, secure materialised views, and secure UDFs. Standard (non-secure) views are not shareable. The consumer mounts the share as a read-only database in their account.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Data Exchange and the Snowflake Marketplace?
cards.a: The Snowflake Marketplace is a public, global listing where any Snowflake account can publish or discover data products. A Data Exchange is a private, invitation-only sharing hub — organisations create their own exchange for a defined group of partners or internal business units.

cards.q: Does data sharing in Snowflake involve copying data between accounts?
cards.a: No. Secure Data Sharing is a live pointer to the provider's data stored in their account. The consumer's virtual warehouse queries the provider's micro-partitions directly — there is no ETL or duplication. Data is always current.

cards.q: What is database replication in Snowflake used for?
cards.a: Replicating a Snowflake database to a secondary account in a different region or cloud provider. Used for: disaster recovery / failover, read-scale distribution, and moving data closer to users in other geographies.

cards.q: What is the difference between Snowpipe and COPY INTO for continuous ingestion?
cards.a: COPY INTO runs in a user-managed warehouse on demand or on schedule — suited for large, batch loads. Snowpipe uses Snowflake-managed (serverless) compute and triggers automatically when files arrive — suited for near-real-time micro-batch ingestion with low operational overhead.

cards.q: How does Snowpipe handle duplicate files?
cards.a: Snowpipe tracks file metadata (path + ETag) and skips files that were already loaded within the past 64 days. To force reload a file, you must either rename it, change its content (changing ETag), or use the COPY INTO command with FORCE=TRUE.

cards.q: What is the Kafka Connector for Snowflake and how does it ingest data?
cards.a: A Kafka Connect plugin that continuously reads messages from Kafka topics and writes them to Snowflake tables (via Snowpipe or INSERT). Each Kafka record becomes a VARIANT row in a Snowflake table. Supports exactly-once delivery using offset tracking.

cards.q: What is an append-only stream and when should you use it?
cards.a: A stream type that only captures INSERT operations — it ignores UPDATEs and DELETEs. More storage-efficient than a standard stream because the change tracking overhead is lower. Use it on insert-only source tables such as event logs, audit tables, or Snowpipe landing tables.

cards.q: How do you build a task DAG in Snowflake?
cards.a: Create a root task with a CRON schedule and child tasks with AFTER <parent_task>. Child tasks run when their parent succeeds. Use ALTER TASK ... RESUME to activate each task (root last). The DAG is visualised in Snowsight under the task definition.

cards.q: What is the maximum number of child tasks per root task (task DAG) in Snowflake?
cards.a: 1,000 tasks in a single DAG (as of current limits). Root task can have multiple direct children, each of which can have their own children.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Dynamic Table and how does it differ from a stream+task pipeline?
cards.a: A Dynamic Table is a declarative, automatically refreshed materialisation: you write the transformation SQL; Snowflake tracks dependencies, determines changed data, and refreshes it. A stream+task pipeline is imperative: you write the CDC logic yourself. Dynamic Tables simplify pipeline code but offer less control over exactly when/how changes are applied.

cards.q: What is TARGET_LAG in a Dynamic Table?
cards.a: Specifies the acceptable freshness lag: how far behind the Dynamic Table can be relative to its source data. Snowflake refreshes the table at a rate needed to stay within this lag. Setting 'DOWNSTREAM' means the lag is inherited from downstream Dynamic Tables.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Standard stream and an Insert-only stream on an external table?
cards.a: Standard streams on regular tables capture INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. External table streams are insert-only by nature (external files are immutable) — they track which new files have been added to the external stage, enabling incremental processing of data-lake files.

cards.q: How do you implement idempotent incremental loads in Snowflake using streams?
cards.a: Use MERGE (not INSERT) when consuming the stream: match on a primary key, update matched rows, insert new rows. Because MERGE is atomic and streams track consumed changes, re-running the task will not double-insert — the stream will be empty unless new changes have arrived.

cards.q: What is COPY INTO <location> (unloading) and what formats does it support?
cards.a: Exports query results or table data to a Snowflake internal stage or external cloud storage. Supports CSV, JSON, Parquet. Options include HEADER (add column names), PARTITION BY (create sub-folders), MAX_FILE_SIZE, and compression.

cards.q: What is the Semi-structured schema detection feature in Snowflake?
cards.a: INFER_SCHEMA() and the related column definitions in COPY INTO auto-detect column names and types from staged Parquet, Avro, or ORC files. You can use CREATE TABLE ... USING TEMPLATE (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*)) FROM TABLE(INFER_SCHEMA(...))) to auto-create a matching table.

cards.q: What is schema evolution in Snowflake COPY INTO?
cards.a: When ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE on a table, COPY INTO will automatically add new columns found in the source files (for semi-structured data) rather than failing. This allows the table schema to evolve as the source adds new fields without manual ALTER TABLE.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Directory Table?
cards.a: Automatically maintained metadata about the files in a stage: file path, size, ETag, last modified time. Accessed via TABLE(@stage). Used in pipeline code to discover and process files efficiently — for example, to find all files added after a given timestamp.

cards.q: How can you monitor Snowpipe ingestion lag and errors?
cards.a: Use SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS() to check pipe state, pending file count, and last loaded time. Query LOAD_HISTORY (information schema) or COPY_HISTORY (account_usage) for per-file load status and error details.

cards.q: What is the role of a Storage Integration in Snowflake?
cards.a: A Snowflake object that stores credentials (IAM role ARN for AWS, service account for GCP, service principal for Azure) for accessing external cloud storage. Stages reference the integration instead of hardcoding access keys — centralising credential management and enabling key rotation without updating every stage.

cards.q: What is Snowpark and how does it relate to data engineering in Snowflake?
cards.a: Snowpark is a developer framework that lets you write data transformation logic in Python, Java, or Scala using a DataFrame API that executes natively inside Snowflake. Data engineers use it to write complex pipeline code that pushes compute to Snowflake, replacing Spark for many use cases.

cards.q: What is a Snowpark Optimised Warehouse?
cards.a: A special warehouse type with 16x more memory per node than a standard warehouse, designed for memory-intensive ML workloads and large Snowpark (Python/Java) operations. Billed at a higher credit rate. Not recommended for standard SQL analytics.

cards.q: What considerations drive the choice of Snowflake cloud provider and region?
cards.a: Data residency and compliance requirements (GDPR, data sovereignty), latency to existing systems and users, colocation with other cloud services (e.g., Kafka on AWS → Snowflake on AWS), pricing differences, and supported features (some features are region-specific).

cards.q: When would you use multiple Snowflake accounts vs. multiple databases within one account?
cards.a: Multiple accounts for: hard isolation (different organisations, strict compliance boundaries, separate billing), cross-cloud deployments, or production/non-production separation with no risk of cross-environment access. Multiple databases within one account for: cost consolidation, shared governance, simpler cross-database queries (no replication needed).

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Organisation and what does it enable?
cards.a: An overarching entity that links multiple Snowflake accounts under a single organisation name. Enables: account-level replication, cross-account cost visibility in ORGANISATION_USAGE, and Snowflake Marketplace publisher identity that spans accounts.

cards.q: How should you design the role hierarchy for a large enterprise Snowflake deployment?
cards.a: Custom functional roles (ANALYST, DATA_ENGINEER, REPORTER) grant object-level privileges. Custom access roles (DB_PROD_READ, DB_PROD_WRITE) own and grant access to specific databases. Functional roles inherit access roles. SYSADMIN sits above custom roles. Never grant ACCOUNTADMIN to functional users.

cards.q: What is the Snowflake Data Governance suite and what features does it include?
cards.a: A set of Enterprise+ features: Dynamic Data Masking (column-level obfuscation), Row Access Policies (row-level filtering), Object Tags (classification labels), Tag-Based Masking (apply masking via tags), Data Classification (auto-suggest tags for PII), Access History (query-level column-read audit log), and Policy Management (centralised policy objects).

cards.q: What is Access History in Snowflake and why is it important for architects?
cards.a: A feature (Enterprise+) that records which columns each query read or modified, who ran the query, and when. Stored in SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY. Used for data lineage audits, PII access monitoring, and compliance reporting.

cards.q: What is Private Connectivity in Snowflake (AWS PrivateLink / Azure Private Link / GCP Private Service Connect)?
cards.a: Routes Snowflake traffic over the cloud provider's private backbone instead of the public internet. Traffic never leaves the provider's network — reducing exposure and satisfying compliance requirements that prohibit public internet data transfer. Requires Business Critical or higher edition.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Data Clean Room?
cards.a: A pattern (using Secure Data Sharing and Secure Views) that lets two parties run joint analyses on combined data without either party seeing the other's raw data. Neither side can extract the other's rows — they can only see aggregated or pre-defined query results.

cards.q: How do you architect cross-region disaster recovery in Snowflake?
cards.a: Use Replication Groups (or Business Critical Failover Groups) to asynchronously replicate specified databases and account objects to a secondary account in a different region. Define an RPO (acceptable data loss) matching your replication schedule, and test failover regularly. Point DNS/connections at the primary account; redirect to secondary on failover.

cards.q: What is the difference between database replication and a Failover Group?
cards.a: Database replication replicates data only. A Failover Group replicates both data AND account objects (users, roles, resource monitors, warehouses, integrations) needed to run a full Snowflake environment on the secondary account. Failover Groups support full account-level DR.

cards.q: What are the RPO and RTO considerations when designing Snowflake HA?
cards.a: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — time between the last replication sync and a failure. Governed by the replication schedule (minimum ~1 minute for some features). RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — time to promote the secondary and redirect connections. Promotion is near-instant in Snowflake; the bottleneck is usually DNS/connection-string updates.

cards.q: How would you design a cost allocation model across business units sharing one Snowflake account?
cards.a: Create one virtual warehouse per business unit (or one per workload type). Apply Resource Monitors per warehouse with per-BU quotas. Tag warehouses with the business unit using Object Tags. Report on usage via ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY filtered by warehouse name or tag. Optionally use separate accounts with cross-account cost reporting via ORGANISATION_USAGE.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Marketplace listing and what can be listed?
cards.a: A published data product on the Snowflake Marketplace. Listings can contain: databases shared via Secure Data Sharing (live data), or Native Apps (applications built on the Snowflake Native App Framework). Listings can be free, paid (via Snowflake billing), or request-only.

cards.q: What is the Snowflake Native App Framework?
cards.a: Allows ISVs and data providers to build applications that run inside a consumer's Snowflake account — not just data shares. Native Apps can include Streamlit UIs, stored procedures, Python UDFs, and reference data. The provider's code runs in the consumer's account but the provider controls what it can access.

cards.q: How does Snowflake handle data lineage at the platform level?
cards.a: Snowflake provides: (1) Access History (column-level read/write tracking). (2) Object Dependencies (SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES shows how views/tasks/pipes reference tables). (3) Dynamic Tables have built-in lineage visualisation in Snowsight. For end-to-end data lineage across tools, integrate with a third-party catalog (e.g., Atlan, Alation, OpenMetadata).

cards.q: What performance patterns should a Snowflake architect consider for a mixed workload (OLAP + ad-hoc + ETL)?
cards.a: Separate virtual warehouses by workload type: large ETL warehouse (L/XL, auto-suspend 5 min), medium analytics warehouse (M, multi-cluster for concurrency), small ad-hoc/BI warehouse (S/XS, auto-suspend 1 min). Use resource monitors per warehouse. Consider a Snowpark-optimised warehouse for ML workloads. Route by application/role using connection strings.

cards.q: What is Snowsight?
cards.a: Snowflake's modern web-based UI (the successor to the Classic Console). It provides SQL worksheets, a query history viewer, database object explorer, dashboards, and admin screens for users, warehouses, and billing — all in the browser.

cards.q: What is SnowSQL?
cards.a: The official command-line client for Snowflake. It connects to Snowflake over TLS, lets you run SQL interactively or in batch mode, and is the only client that supports the PUT and GET commands for transferring files to/from internal stages.

cards.q: What are Snowflake worksheets?
cards.a: Named, saved SQL editing contexts in Snowsight. Each worksheet has its own role, warehouse, database, and schema context. Multiple worksheets can run independently in parallel. Worksheets can be organised into folders and shared with other users.

cards.q: How does Snowflake handle SQL identifier case sensitivity?
cards.a: Unquoted identifiers are stored and compared in UPPERCASE. Double-quoted identifiers preserve exact case and are case-sensitive. Best practice: use unquoted (uppercase) identifiers unless you specifically need mixed-case names.

cards.q: What is AUTOCOMMIT in Snowflake?
cards.a: Snowflake runs with AUTOCOMMIT = TRUE by default — every DML statement is automatically committed unless you explicitly start a transaction with BEGIN. You can disable AUTOCOMMIT at the session level to group statements into manual transactions.

cards.q: What is the Information Schema in Snowflake?
cards.a: An ANSI-standard set of views inside every Snowflake database (INFORMATION_SCHEMA schema) that shows metadata about the objects in that database — tables, columns, views, stages, file formats, etc. Data reflects the current state of that database only.

cards.q: What is ACCOUNT_USAGE in Snowflake and how does it differ from INFORMATION_SCHEMA?
cards.a: ACCOUNT_USAGE is a shared database (SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE) with views covering the entire account — all databases, all warehouses, query history, login history, storage usage, etc. It has a latency of 45 minutes to 3 hours. INFORMATION_SCHEMA is per-database and near real-time but limited to that database's objects.

cards.q: What does the SHOW command do in Snowflake?
cards.a: Lists objects of a given type visible to the current role: SHOW TABLES, SHOW WAREHOUSES, SHOW USERS, SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE my_role, etc. More convenient than querying INFORMATION_SCHEMA for a quick inventory; output can be queried with SELECT * FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())).

cards.q: What are constraints in Snowflake and are they enforced?
cards.a: Snowflake supports PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, and NOT NULL constraints in DDL for documentation and tooling compatibility. Only NOT NULL is enforced at runtime. PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, and FOREIGN KEY are informational only — Snowflake does not reject violating rows.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Secure View and a regular view in Snowflake?
cards.a: A Secure View hides its underlying definition from users who don't own it — the definition is not visible in SHOW VIEWS or INFORMATION_SCHEMA. Required when sharing views via Secure Data Sharing (regular views expose their SQL to data consumers).

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Pipe object?
cards.a: A named object that encapsulates a COPY INTO statement and a source stage. Snowpipe uses the pipe definition to load files as they arrive. The pipe stores the load history used to deduplicate file loads.

cards.q: What is the user stage vs. named internal stage?
cards.a: Every user automatically has a personal user stage (@~) — no creation needed, not shareable, tied to the user. A named internal stage (CREATE STAGE) is a standalone object that can be granted to roles and shared across users and processes. Preferred for production pipelines.

cards.q: What Snowflake data types are used for date and time?
cards.a: DATE (date only), TIME (time only), TIMESTAMP_NTZ (no timezone — stores as-is), TIMESTAMP_LTZ (local timezone — stores UTC, displays in session timezone), TIMESTAMP_TZ (stores offset with the value). TIMESTAMP is an alias for whichever variant the TIMESTAMP_TYPE_MAPPING session parameter specifies (default: NTZ).

cards.q: What is the VARIANT size limit in Snowflake?
cards.a: Each VARIANT value can be up to 16 MB when uncompressed. Individual objects or arrays that exceed this limit cannot be stored in a single VARIANT column — they must be split or truncated before loading.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Alert?
cards.a: A named object that evaluates a condition on a schedule and sends a notification (via a notification integration — email, SNS, PagerDuty, etc.) when the condition is true. Used for data quality monitoring, pipeline failure detection, and threshold alerts.

cards.q: What is the Snowflake Partner Ecosystem?
cards.a: A network of certified technology partners — BI tools (Tableau, Looker, Power BI), ETL/ELT tools (dbt, Fivetran, Matillion, Airbyte), data catalogues (Alation, Atlan), and security tools — that have native, certified connectors to Snowflake. Listed on the Snowflake Partner Connect page.

cards.q: What is a Notification Integration in Snowflake?
cards.a: A Snowflake object that connects Snowflake to an external messaging service (AWS SNS, Azure Event Grid, GCP Pub/Sub, email). Used by Alerts, Snowpipe error notifications, and Tasks to send messages outside Snowflake.

cards.q: What is an Event Table in Snowflake?
cards.a: A special table that stores log and trace events emitted from Snowflake handler code (Python UDFs, stored procedures, Snowpark). Replaces the need for external logging — you query the event table with SQL to see errors, log messages, and OpenTelemetry spans from your code.

cards.q: What are External Functions in Snowflake?
cards.a: User-defined functions that call an external HTTPS endpoint (an API Gateway backed by AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, or GCP Cloud Functions). The SQL query passes rows to the external service and receives results back. Useful for enrichment, ML inference, or third-party API calls.

cards.q: What is the Query Acceleration Service (QAS) in Snowflake?
cards.a: A serverless feature that offloads parts of an eligible query (large scans, outlier partitions) to additional serverless compute rather than requiring you to upsize the warehouse. Useful for queries with variable data skew. Enabled per-warehouse with ENABLE_QUERY_ACCELERATION = TRUE.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Budget?
cards.a: A newer (2023+) account-level spending control object that sets a monthly credit spending limit for a group of Snowflake objects or the whole account. More granular than Resource Monitors — Budgets can monitor serverless feature costs (clustering, Tasks, Snowpipe) that Resource Monitors cannot.

cards.q: What are Future Grants in Snowflake?
cards.a: A privilege grant applied to all future objects of a type in a schema or database: GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA mydb.myschema TO ROLE analyst. New tables created after the grant automatically receive the privilege — no need to re-grant on each new object.

cards.q: What is GRANT OWNERSHIP in Snowflake and when would you use it?
cards.a: Transfers ownership of an object from one role to another: GRANT OWNERSHIP ON TABLE orders TO ROLE data_engineer. Needed when migrating objects between teams, or when the creating role should not retain long-term ownership. Only the current owner or ACCOUNTADMIN can transfer ownership.

cards.q: What is External Tokenization in Snowflake?
cards.a: A column-level security pattern where sensitive values are replaced with tokens by an external vault (e.g., Protegrity, Voltage) before landing in Snowflake. A masking policy calls an External Function to de-tokenize values at query time for authorised users. Data at rest is never in plaintext.

cards.q: What is Data Classification in Snowflake?
cards.a: A system that automatically scans column values and metadata and suggests privacy tags (e.g., NAME, EMAIL, PHONE, SSN) that can then be applied via Object Tags. Helps teams identify PII/sensitive data without manually reviewing every column.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Network Rule?
cards.a: A newer (2023+) object that defines a set of IP ranges or VPC IDs as an allowed or blocked group. Network Rules are referenced by Network Policies, replacing the flat allowed/blocked IP list with reusable, composable rule objects.

cards.q: What are Iceberg Tables in Snowflake?
cards.a: Tables that store data in the Apache Iceberg open-table format on customer-managed cloud storage, while using Snowflake as the query engine. Enables a data lakehouse pattern: open format data readable by other engines (Spark, Flink), governed and queried through Snowflake.

cards.q: What is Snowflake Cortex?
cards.a: A suite of serverless AI/ML features built into Snowflake: Cortex LLM Functions (COMPLETE, SUMMARIZE, TRANSLATE, SENTIMENT, CLASSIFY_TEXT using hosted LLMs), Cortex ML Functions (FORECAST, ANOMALY_DETECTION using AutoML), and Cortex Search (vector search). Runs entirely within Snowflake — no data leaves the platform.

cards.q: What is the RESULT_SCAN function in Snowflake?
cards.a: Returns the output of a previous query as a table using its query ID: SELECT * FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())). Useful for processing SHOW command output or inspecting results of VALIDATE statements in subsequent SQL.

cards.q: What is the difference between TIMESTAMP_NTZ, TIMESTAMP_LTZ, and TIMESTAMP_TZ?
cards.a: TIMESTAMP_NTZ — stores date/time with no timezone; displayed exactly as stored. TIMESTAMP_LTZ — stores as UTC; displayed in the session's local timezone (TIMEZONE parameter). TIMESTAMP_TZ — stores the value plus an explicit UTC offset; preserves the original timezone information.

cards.q: What is a Stored Procedure owner's rights vs. caller's rights in Snowflake?
cards.a: Owner's rights (default): the procedure runs with the privileges of the role that owns it, not the caller. The caller only needs EXECUTE PRIVILEGE — they can't see or access objects they don't have direct grants to. Caller's rights: the procedure runs with the caller's role — useful when you want the procedure to respect the caller's access level.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Task with a CRON schedule and a serverless Task?
cards.a: A warehouse-based Task runs on a specified virtual warehouse (you pay for warehouse time even if the task is fast). A serverless Task (WAREHOUSE = omitted, USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE specified) uses Snowflake-managed compute — you pay per compute-second used, and Snowflake auto-sizes based on prior run history.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake SEQUENCE and what guarantees does it make?
cards.a: A sequence generates unique integer values with NEXTVAL. Values are guaranteed unique and monotonically increasing, but NOT gap-free — gaps can occur due to rollbacks, multi-session access, or batch allocation. Do not rely on sequences for dense, contiguous numbering.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Materialized View and a Dynamic Table in Snowflake?
cards.a: Materialized Views are automatically refreshed by Snowflake when base data changes, but have significant limitations: no JOINs on non-shared-micropartitions, no subqueries, Enterprise+ only. Dynamic Tables support full SQL (JOINs, CTEs, aggregations), have configurable lag, and can form dependency chains. Dynamic Tables are the recommended modern approach.

cards.q: What is the difference between an internal named stage and a user/table stage?
cards.a: User stage (@~) and table stage (@%tablename) are auto-created, not grantable, and tied to a user or table. Named stages (CREATE STAGE) are independent objects, can be granted to roles, support custom file format defaults, and are the recommended approach for production pipelines.

cards.q: What is columnar storage and why does Snowflake use it?
cards.a: Columnar storage organises data by column rather than by row. This means analytic queries that read only a few columns scan far less data. It also enables much higher compression ratios within a column (similar values together). Snowflake's micro-partitions are stored in a compressed columnar format (based on PAX/hybrid).

cards.q: What happens to old micro-partitions when data is updated or deleted in Snowflake?
cards.a: Micro-partitions are immutable. An UPDATE or DELETE creates new micro-partitions with the changed/surviving rows and marks the old micro-partitions as deleted. The old partitions are retained for the Time Travel retention period, then moved to Fail-Safe, and eventually purged.

cards.q: What is the Continuous Data Protection (CDP) lifecycle in Snowflake?
cards.a: The layered protection Snowflake provides automatically: 1. Operational storage (current data). 2. Time Travel (user-accessible historical queries/restores, up to 90 days). 3. Fail-Safe (7-day Snowflake-managed emergency recovery after Time Travel). No additional configuration required.

cards.q: How many databases can a single Snowflake account have?
cards.a: There is no documented hard limit on the number of databases per account. Snowflake accounts can contain thousands of databases, schemas, and tables. Practical limits are driven by governance and cost, not platform constraints.

cards.q: Can a Snowflake Virtual Warehouse span multiple cloud regions?
cards.a: No. A virtual warehouse runs entirely within the cloud region of the Snowflake account. Cross-region compute is not possible within a single warehouse. Cross-region data access requires replication.

cards.q: What types of objects can be cloned in Snowflake?
cards.a: Databases, schemas, tables (permanent, temporary, transient), streams, sequences, file formats, stages (named internal), tasks, and pipes. Cloning a schema or database recursively clones all supported child objects.

cards.q: What is the relationship between a Snowflake account and an organisation?
cards.a: An Organisation is an optional grouping of multiple Snowflake accounts under one entity. It enables cross-account replication, account-level transfers, and consolidated usage reporting in ORGANISATION_USAGE. A single account can exist without an organisation.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Worksheet's context and why does it matter?
cards.a: Each worksheet has a role, warehouse, database, and schema set as its context. SQL runs with that role's privileges, against that database/schema (used as the default for unqualified object names), using that warehouse. Changing context mid-session affects all subsequent statements in that worksheet.

cards.q: What is INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY and what does it contain?
cards.a: A table function in every database's INFORMATION_SCHEMA that returns query history for the current user (or all users if ACCOUNTADMIN/SYSADMIN). Returns up to 7 days of history. For longer history, use SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY (up to 365 days, ~45 min latency).

cards.q: What is the ORGADMIN role in Snowflake?
cards.a: A special account-level role (granted only by Snowflake) that can manage the Organisation — create accounts, view organisation-level usage, and enable cross-account features. It is separate from ACCOUNTADMIN and typically held by only one account per organisation.

cards.q: What is a Snowflake Session Policy?
cards.a: An object that controls session timeout behaviour — idle timeout and maximum session duration. Applied at user or account level. Useful for enforcing inactivity-based session termination for compliance.

cards.q: What is the difference between GRANT PRIVILEGE and GRANT ROLE?
cards.a: GRANT PRIVILEGE (e.g., GRANT SELECT ON TABLE t TO ROLE r) gives a role the ability to perform a specific action on a specific object. GRANT ROLE (GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE manager) adds a role to another role's or user's role hierarchy — the grantee inherits all privileges of the granted role.

cards.q: What does GRANT ... WITH GRANT OPTION do?
